content_list.content_text: In 2014, Steve McQueen (b. 1969) made history as the first Black person to lift the Best Picture statuette, for his work on 12 Years a Slave (2013). In 2018, Jordan Peele (b. 1979) became the first Black person to win the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay, for Get Out (2017). In 2002, Halle Berry (b. 1966) became the first Black actress to take home the Oscar for Best Actress, for Monster's Ball (2001).

content_list.title: Sexuality and Identity
content_list.description:
Sexuality, ethnicity, social status, life chances, surrender to drugs, crime, prejudice, bullying. All of these urgent, current issues are richly and beautifully addressed in the delicate and deeply personal Moonlight, the second feature film by Barry Jenkins, who also wrote the screenplay based on a work by playwright Tarell Alvin McCraney. But perhaps, above all, what stays with the viewer when the credits start to roll is a profound sense of the search for identity, a universal theme toward which all the other aspects elegantly converge.

Told in three chapters, each covering a key moment in the life of Chiron, from his childhood to adulthood, the film weaves together socially relevant themes and invites us to reflect on our own formation, on our choices versus the social determinism that can keep us from truly choosing a path of our own, a true one, that starts mainly from within ourselves. While Chiron suffers all kinds of abuse, finding his only "role model" in a drug dealer who takes him in when he is very young, Jenkins, unhurried, stitches together an engaging and deeply rich narrative that deals with the most diverse subjects in a fluid and realistic way, never resorting to didacticism or even pausing so that the viewer can fully fill in the "gaps" left by the two significant time jumps he makes without ceremony, swapping the actors who play Chiron in the process.

It is particularly fascinating how skillfully Jenkins introduces us to Chiron three times in a row without needing many words. The production design – notably the costumes – and the direction of the actors deserve special mention here, as they build perfect bridges from one moment to the next that let us navigate the protagonist's life fluidly and surely, without feeling any hiccup. In fact, it would be fairer to say that we don't feel any hiccup too strongly, because the work of the director and screenwriter here makes us long to know more about Chiron, that is, about every element we are frantically forced to try to fill in with our imagination between each time jump.

But Jenkins never hands us what we want on a silver platter. No flashbacks. No lingering look at the past. The film strides forward exactly like life. If we blink, a year goes by. If we sleep, a decade goes by. And who we are becomes an amalgam of influences, good and bad, external and internal, conflicting and harmonious, over every day of our lives, lives that may very well be represented on several fronts by Chiron and his struggle to understand exactly who he is, who he should be and who he becomes.

However, there are no definitive answers, much less easy ones. What there is are questions, perhaps glimpses of what will be and what might have been, but never explanations or moments that take the viewer by the hand to lead them down a smoother path. In Moonlight, the goal is to present slices of the life of a young man who is, himself, a slice of society, at once reflecting the reality of many and miles away from the reality of so many others. But there is a convergence in the narrative glue of the search for identity, something that, time and again, at some point in life, affects everyone, even the most self-assured.

In the first third of the film, Chiron – or Little – is played by Alex Hibbert with a shyness and innocence that are truly impressive, befitting his small, fragile frame. The boy runs from bullies at school and ends up entering the life of crack dealer Juan, in a small but unforgettable turn by Mahershala Ali (n-1974), who more than justifies his Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Actor by handling two opposites so perfectly: his hard street persona and the persona full of the affection he comes to feel for the lost boy. We see, in a succession of sequences interspersed with slight jumps in time, the two growing closer and the father figure Juan becomes for Little, even considering the obvious conflict with his mother Paula (Naomie Harris, also living up to her Oscar nomination), who is addicted to the same drugs Juan sells.

Just as we are getting used to Little's drama, Jenkins makes his first time cut, taking us a few years into the future, with Chiron now actually called Chiron, already a teenager and played by Ashton Sanders. His daily problems with bullies and his increasingly addicted mother continue, but his sexuality begins to come more strongly into play, something only touched upon in the sequences with Little. From then on, the events are at once tender and frightening, and they contribute to our understanding of the final third, shorter and more direct, when we see Chiron as an adult, now simply called Black (Trevante Rhodes) and completely transformed physically. Here, perhaps in symbolic moments before the first day of the rest of his life, we see a beautiful movement by the character in search of a past he left behind but never forgot, closing the narrative circle in exemplary fashion.

The screenplay is built from the "stacking" of Chiron's experiences. With each new "incarnation" of the character, we understand exactly how he got to where he is and what each action means to him and to those around him. In less skillful hands, the story could easily have become tiresome, perhaps even repetitive, but Moonlight is precisely the opposite. Each segment brings information that we want and that we find all too little, always wanting to witness every minute of the young man's life and unconsciously transporting ourselves – as far as possible and based on each person's experiences – into that setting. It is life as it is, but in a poetic way, with a light, discreet layer of fable in the sense of the universality of feelings and actions.

And, of course, besides Ali, Harris and Janelle Monáe (as Teresa, Juan's girlfriend), who are already worth the price of admission, there is the Hibbert/Sanders/Rhodes trio, who should collectively compete for the Best Actor Oscar for their flawless portrayal of Chiron in his three phases. Even though the screenplay takes great care to make us believe in the transitions and changes of age, it is only through the work of the three that the intention becomes reality, even considering the most radical change, when the scrawny young man transforms into Black, an inevitable persona created by the conditions around him and naturally inspired by the young man's past.

The artistic care lavished on Moonlight helps the film reach a beautiful and rare status of realist poetry in motion that does not rely on transcendental approaches or contemplative cinematography to achieve its goal. Experienced cinematographer James Laxton (Yoga Hosers) takes care to keep the film with both feet on the ground, at the same time evoking an air that verges on a documentary atmosphere and plunging into hypnotic and somewhat ghostly colors in the night shots, notably those bathed in the moonlight of the title, which carries so much symbolism. The same can be said of the contribution of Nicholas Britell (The Big Short) with his absolutely captivating, classically inclined score, full of beautiful strings that Jenkins efficiently synchronizes with the picture so that it only underlines feelings rather than dictating them. The end result is, without fear of being wrong, one of the most beautiful scores of 2016.

Moonlight is an unforgettable intimate spectacle that will touch each viewer in a different way. If the film can be seen as being about the search for an identity, it never loses its own, striding toward an uncertain future, but one full of life, choices, impositions and, yes, love.

content_list.content_text: And not without reason. A year earlier, in 2015, Selma (2014) was completely ignored at the awards, despite its top score from hundreds of critics. Ava DuVernay (b. 1972) — who would later direct When They See Us, once again being snubbed by the Golden Globes — came nowhere near a Best Director nomination, and David Oyelowo (b. 1976), despite his highly praised performance, also received no nomination.

information.contentText: Oyelowo, who played Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. in the film, said that members of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences objected when members of the "Selma" cast protested the death of a Black American months before the film's release. "I remember at the premiere of 'Selma,' us wearing 'I Can't Breathe' T-shirts in protest," Oyelowo said, referring to the death of Eric Garner in New York after he was detained. Garner died in July 2014 and "Selma" premiered in December 2014. "Academy members called into the studio and our producers saying, 'How dare they do that? Why are they stirring shit up?' and 'We are not going to vote for that film because we do not think it is their place to be doing that.'" Oyelowo and director Ava DuVernay were left out of the 2015 Oscar nominations, helping to spur the #OscarsSoWhite campaign demanding greater diversity in Hollywood. "Selma" won only the Oscar for Best Original Song.

content_list.title: Greta Gerwig Writes What She Knows (and She Knows a Lot)
content_list.description: Over the last decade, Greta Gerwig has transformed from an indie darling on screen into one of cinema's most promising filmmakers. While it's clear that she shares certain styles and tastes with Noah Baumbach – her real-life partner and creative collaborator on Frances Ha and Mistress America – the 2017 film Lady Bird, which Gerwig wrote and directed, established her as one of the strongest storytelling voices in the industry. Loosely based on Gerwig's upbringing in Sacramento, Lady Bird stars Saoirse Ronan as the protagonist, who must leave "the Midwest of California" to live up to her self-given persona. Through Gerwig's screenplay, however, one begins to discover that unresolved family dysfunction is the primary conflict. Act by act, Gerwig pays homage to her cinematic influences while showcasing her lively writing voice and her ability to craft an impactful scene. Lady Bird feels organic, but it is Gerwig's meticulous structure and attention to detail that ensure people of all ages, demographics and genders can relate to it in some way.

content_list.content_text: In the year the hashtags emerged, the situation was even worse. In 2016, the famous official photo of the Oscar nominees went viral for the absence of any Black people. And most importantly: contrary to some arguments that dismiss the lack of diversity, there was no shortage of opportunities. In the acting categories alone, for example, Idris Elba (b. 1972) was ignored for his role in Beasts of No Nation (2015) and Samuel L. Jackson (b. 1948) was left out for The Hateful Eight (2015).

At the time, George Clooney (b. 1961) — one of the many supporters of the 2016 boycott of the ceremony — raised what may be the most important point so far: the problem is rooted in the industry. While few leading roles are offered to Black people, many of them are still stuck in the same stereotypes. It's worth remembering, after all, that of the 34 Black women nominated for Best Actress, 20 were for roles as slaves or maids. Almost two thirds.

content_list.title: Strength and Affection in Little Women
content_list.description:
Despite being present in six categories at the 2020 Oscars, the Best Picture nomination for Little Women took many people by surprise, since the film had not appeared at other awards. However, this is in no way a demerit nor does it diminish its quality, since the new adaptation of the novel written by Louisa May Alcott is an enchanting story of struggle and love, in every possible meaning of those words.

Directed by Greta Gerwig, the film essentially revolves around four sisters: Josephine "Jo" March (Saoirse Ronan), Margaret "Meg" March (Emma Watson), Elizabeth "Beth" March (Eliza Scanlen) and Amy March (Florence Pugh). Daughters of Marmee March (Laura Dern), they live their ordinary lives without great luxuries while the United States goes through the Civil War, in which their father (Bob Odenkirk) is one of the soldiers. While they wait for the return of the only man of the house, the young women, all connected to the artistic world in some way, must deal with Beth's illness, as she faces a disease she had overcome but which returned even stronger.

The events of the film unfold over a period of seven years, between the end of the war and the first years after it. To tell what happens over the years, the director opts for a narrative that constantly travels between present and past. Although this causes some confusion right at the start of the film, partly due to the excessive use of cuts, which makes the direction present too much information to the audience, Gerwig soon finds her footing and turns this shifting timeline into one of the main strengths of her work.

To mark the past, when the family, though anxious about the father's presence in the war, lives mostly happy moments, with the girls full of adolescent energy and Beth healthy, the director chooses extremely vibrant colors both in the characters' costumes and throughout the mise-en-scène. In addition, saturation is pushed quite high, creating a strong impression of vivacity in every scene.

With the present, however, the opposite happens. The screen is taken over by cold colors and dark tones, as well as low saturation, bringing sadness and coldness to the film, which grow even stronger in the many scenes amid great amounts of snow.

These back-and-forths in time also resonate with the events of the story. For example, the relationship of Theodore "Laurie" Laurence (Timothée Chalamet) with the March sisters could easily be described this way. Being a charming, wealthy young man, Laurie, even though Jo is his great love, makes some advance, to a greater or lesser degree, toward all the March sisters except Beth.

It is also interesting to see how each artistic field influences the shaping of each character's personality. Take Ronan's character, for example. An avid reader, Jo March writes short stories and novels and dreams of becoming a great writer. With a strong personality, and even called a boy after a certain incident, she goes to New York with the goal of getting her writing published. However, she runs into the blatant sexism of the time, in which nothing she writes is good enough, since her stories have strong female characters as protagonists and "that doesn't sell" because "it's too heroic" and "it lacks romance". Despite these adversities, her questioning, unstoppable drive keeps her moving forward, showing the influence of books on her upbringing and her enormous determination.

Another extremely important element in the film is the score. Present throughout practically the entire running time, Alexandre Desplat's composition is essential to conveying all the emotion of the narrative. Sometimes building gradually and at other times bursting in with great fury, Desplat turns small moments into major events, fully justifying his nomination for Best Original Score.

It is impossible not to comment on the costumes, so important for a period film. Although absolutely beautiful, the garments created by Jacqueline Durran stand out above all for their colors. Working in perfect harmony with the color palette, the costumes help identify feelings and personalities, as when, after a sad event, we see Marmee March entirely in black except for a red scarf around her neck, marking not only her love for that person but also her loving nature.

Little Women is a visually enchanting work with a great narrative, which exposes the difficulties faced by women in the 19th century, raised with the sole purpose of marrying, without giving up on romance. A high-quality blend of struggle and love by Greta Gerwig.

My grandmother, who lived to be 100 years young, was a college graduate even though her mother was a slave. She saved years of Social Security checks and put me through NYU. Before the world tonight, I give praise to our ancestors who built this country, along with those who suffered genocide. The ancestors who will help us regain our humanity. content_list.content_title: The dynasty of Mexican directors at the Oscars

information.contentTitle: The Three Amigos: Alejandro González Iñárritu, Guillermo del Toro and Alfonso Cuarón
information.contentText: Through 2019, overall, five of the six Best Director Oscars went to the friends (Damien Chazelle was the exception in 2016) – Cuarón, Guillermo del Toro and Alejandro González Iñárritu, often referred to as "the Three Amigos" of cinema.

content_list.content_text: Long before Cuarón, Alejandro González Iñárritu – Birdman or (The Unexpected Virtue of Ignorance) (2014), The Revenant (2015) – and Guillermo del Toro – The Shape of Water (2017) – won Oscar statuettes for their work as directors, it was practically unthinkable to see anyone other than an American or a European come out on top as director — women, Black people, Asians and people of other ethnicities underrepresented in the media as a whole can attest to that, but let's leave that subject for another time. However, when the Three Amigos, as Cuarón, Iñárritu and del Toro are known, built the bridge from Mexico City to Hollywood back in the 2000s, it soon became clear that the trio could reach heights and levels previously impossible and improbable.

Even though, among Latin American countries, Mexico has always had the strongest presence at the ceremony of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences of the United States, it took a while for Mexicans to find their first chances of true relevance, from the perspective of popular taste, to shine at the prestigious ceremony — artists from the country had previously been nominated as art directors, such as the acclaimed Emile Kuri (1907-2000) and Edward Carrere (1906-1984). It was only at the 25th edition of the awards (1953) that a triumph came in one of the Oscars' main categories: Anthony Quinn (1915-2001) as Best Supporting Actor for Viva Zapata! (1952), in a win over Hollywood's own Richard Burton (1925-1984) and Jack Palance (1919-2006).

content_list.title: Guillermo del Toro - Monsters, Makeup & Movie Magic
content_list.description: A video showing why Guillermo del Toro is one of the greatest directors working today, highlighting his direction and how his monsters manage to be different.

content_list.content_text: The success of the everlasting Zorba the Greek — the role that would earn Quinn his second Best Actor Oscar nomination, in 1965, after Wild Is the Wind (1957) — placed him alongside José Ferrer (1912-1992), an actor of Puerto Rican origin, the two of them being the only Latinos up to that point to take home at least one golden statuette: Quinn would double his feat with a supporting actor win for Lust for Life (1956), while Ferrer won his trophy in 1951, for Cyrano de Bergerac (1950). On the women's side, Katy Jurado (1924-2002), a star of the golden age of Mexican cinema between the 1940s and 1950s, also received a supporting actress Oscar nomination, for Broken Lance (1954).

But all these brief, albeit important, achievements concerned Mexico as seen by the cinema of the United States, a situation that changed when the first two Latin American titles, originating from the southernmost part of the North American continent, were nominated for Best Foreign Language Film: we're talking about Macario (1960) and Ánimas Trujano (The Important Man, 1961), classics of Mexican cinema that made Mexico join the usual powerhouses France, Italy, Japan and Sweden in the annual races for the gold medal for non-English-language features. And both got there by going beyond the traditional melodrama of Mexican productions of the time.

information.contentText: Pacific Rim is intended as a tribute to Japanese films featuring gigantic creatures. Director Guillermo del Toro describes his film as "a beautiful poem to giant monsters".

content_list.content_text: There were two main influences, even if indirect, on these nominees, who would soon be followed in the 1960s by Brazil's own The Given Word (1962) and the also Mexican Tlayucan (1962). First, the film movements that emerged in France and Italy, which took the seventh art out of the studios to bring it closer to the reality, particularly the social reality, of the post-World War II world; and second, a singular figure, of Spanish origin but based in Mexico between 1946 and 1960 after numerous political persecutions: the director and screenwriter Luis Buñuel (1900-1983), one of the masters of cinema, best known for masterpieces such as El ángel exterminador (The Exterminating Angel, 1962) and Belle de jour (1967).

The filmmaker, who despite having shot French and Spanish works in the '60s and '70s, for which he was twice nominated for the Oscar for Best Screenplay, chose Mexico as his home until his death. There, he had the opportunity not only to expand his own art but also to influence local production. Exploring more realistic themes, albeit through his surrealist lens — Buñuel was, alongside his former friend, the painter Salvador Dalí (1904-1989), one of the forerunners of that artistic movement —, the director brought the streets and greater psychological depth to Mexican filmmaking, which until then had concentrated on melodramas, comedies, musicals, and noir and horror features. Low-budget productions, in short.

information.contentTitle: Bastidores de O Regresso: o diretor

content_list.title: How Kubrick, Spielberg, and Inarritu Stage their Scenes
content_list.description: An essay on staging and blocking your scenes, like Spielberg's Minority Report, Kubrick's A Clockwork Orange and Iñárritu's Birdman.

content_list.content_text: Questioning the power of the Catholic Church in his works, promoting female leads within a sexist, macho culture and, above all, offering pointed analyses of Mexico's social inequalities in his anti-bourgeois films, Buñuel helped cement Mexico's position on the world film map and also became a point of reference for filmmakers of later generations. And although the extensions of the Spaniard's art are more visible in the cinema of filmmakers such as Pedro Almodóvar (b. 1949) and Miguel Gomes (b. 1972), the concern with reality, the allegorical character and the constant mixing of truth and fantasy are present in the works of the Three Amigos.

Mexican participation at the Oscars, and Latin American participation as a whole, however, went into decline after these early successes. Mexico and Latin America as a whole would only return in full force around the 1990s, the decade in which — not by chance — Cuarón, del Toro and Iñárritu began shooting their feature films. The comeback would finally come in the race for the Best Cinematography statuette, 30 years after the original nomination of Gabriel Figueroa (1907-1997) for the visuals of The Night of the Iguana (1964), with none other than three-time winner Emmanuel Lubezki (b. 1964) in the running for the cinematography award: in 1996 the artist received the first of his 8 Oscar nominations for A Little Princess (1995), directed by Cuarón.

information.contentText: The shoot lasted 9 months and took place in Canada and Argentina, in sub-zero temperatures. The crew was practically chasing the snow, and everyone had to keep traveling constantly to wherever it was coldest. The harsh winter and the constant travel led some crew members to quit the job.

content_list.title: How Alfonso Cuarón makes every shot count
content_list.description: A video essay highlighting Alfonso's skill with long takes, and how every frame matters.

content_list.content_text: Chivo, the nickname by which Lubezki is best known in the industry, became a personal friend of the Roma filmmaker back in their teens, when the two attended the same classes at the film school of the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), the country's most important university. They began their partnership back in the 1980s, the same period in which del Toro, Iñárritu and cinematographer Rodrigo Prieto (n-1965) — today a direct collaborator of Martin Scorsese (n-1942) — also started shooting in the capital. Together, these artists forged a friendship and a professional relationship of mutual support at a time when Mexican cinema had been pushed aside by the telenovela boom.

This collaborative environment of creative support reached a first peak in 2007, when Cuarón, del Toro and Iñárritu received their first direct Oscar nominations — the first two in the Best Original Screenplay category for Children of Men (2006) and El laberinto del fauno (Pan's Labyrinth, 2006), and the last as director and producer of Babel (2006); but all three would lose. Despite these defeats, however, the Three Amigos — alongside other nominees from previous years such as Fernanda Montenegro (n-1929), Benicio del Toro (n-1967), Catalina Sandino Moreno (n-1981), Salma Hayek (n-1966) and director Fernando Meirelles (n-1955) — helped tear down the barriers that kept Latinos away from awards like the Oscars.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from The Shape of Water
information.contentText: Anyone who follows Guillermo del Toro's filmography knows his films are full of fantastic creatures. Besides working with sensational makeup artists, the director has actor Doug Jones as his right-hand man. In the Hellboy films, Jones played Abe Sapien and the Angel of Death; in Pan's Labyrinth he brought to life the Pale Man (that monster with eyes in the palms of his hands) and the mythological creature that gives the film its name. Guess who Guillermo del Toro cast to play the amphibious being in The Shape of Water? And do you know how long his makeup took to apply? More than three hours!

content_list.content_text: After all, artists from Latin America and their descendants have obviously always been part of Hollywood in one way or another, the American film industry being, of course, an offshoot of society as a whole. A brief historical, cultural and even political digression is in order here: during the 20th century, above all, the wave of Latin American immigration to the US expanded at full steam, a runaway increase that generated an increasingly pointed response: Hispanophobia or Latinophobia, a sentiment that encompasses fear, aversion, hatred and discrimination, among other negative reactions, against Latin American peoples in the North American giant.

We mention this social phenomenon — recently intensified by the election of Donald Trump to the presidency of the United States, a Republican politician who makes no secret of his xenophobia, especially in his already infamous attempt to build a wall on the border with Mexico to keep Mexicans out — because it bears directly on the victories of Cuarón, Iñárritu and del Toro. As deserved as they may be from a technical, artistic and cinematic standpoint, the Three Amigos' triumphs as directors at the Academy Awards (for Gravity, Birdman, The Revenant and The Shape of Water, respectively) are also a clear political statement by the institution amid the current state of affairs.

information.contentText: The film was shot so that it would appear to have been made entirely in one single take, with the exception of the images that open the feature. This was an idea Iñárritu had from the very beginning, even though cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki believed the shooting time needed for such an approach would be impossible with older technologies.

content_list.title: How Alfonso Cuarón shot 'Roma's' beach scene in one take
content_list.description: Besides serving as writer, director and producer, Alfonso Cuarón was also the cinematographer on the Best Picture nominee "Roma". For Variety's Artisans series, he explained why he knew the film couldn't be "a nostalgic, old-school black-and-white example".

movie.overview: In 1970s Mexico City, two domestic workers help a mother of four while her husband is away for an extended period of time.
movie.tagline: There are periods in history that scar societies and moments in life that transform us as individuals.
movie.title: Roma

content_list.content_text: Although the Academy remains a mostly white and male organization, as described at the beginning of this analysis, the recent inclusion of greater diversity within the institution's ranks has been changing the landscape, even if only to a certain extent. These are gradual gains for minorities who — as author Ioan Grillo points out in his New York Times article on the Three Amigos' success at the Oscars — are gaining ground and showing, even if only through the wins of Cuarón, del Toro and Iñárritu for now, that their participation in Hollywood is a "reminder of how ethnic and cultural diversity can enrich the film industry"; and not only that industry, of course.

information.contentText: The film was praised by filmmaker James Cameron, who said: "I think it's the best space photography ever done, I think it's the best space film ever done, and it's the movie I've been hungry to see for an awfully long time."

content_list.content_text: Roma is, in short, one more stone in the building of the dynasty of Mexican directors at the Oscars, who not only established a quantitative hegemony but also created a platform that solidifies the Latino presence in the commercial seventh art of the United States. It is a tiny triumph when placed in the context of the nearly century-old Academy and the capitalist nature of Hollywood, but it is still a meaningful victory in promoting greater diversity and representation at a time when minorities have been suffering harsh setbacks. And the Mexican glory is also Latin American glory, which — we must not forget, though we almost always do — by extension is ours too.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the article "A dinastia dos diretores mexicanos no Oscar" (The Dynasty of Mexican Directors at the Oscars), by Renato Furtado

movies.overview: The tender, heartbreaking story of a young man’s struggle to find himself, told across three defining chapters in his life as he experiences the ecstasy, pain, and beauty of falling in love, while grappling with his own sexuality.
movies.title: Moonlight

movies.overview: In 1970s Mexico City, two domestic workers help a mother of four while her husband is away for an extended period of time.
movies.title: Roma

movies.original_title: Birdman or (The Unexpected Virtue of Ignorance)
movies.overview: A fading actor best known for his portrayal of a popular superhero attempts to mount a comeback by appearing in a Broadway play. As opening night approaches, his attempts to become more altruistic, rebuild his career, and reconnect with friends and family prove more difficult than expected.
movies.title: Birdman or (The Unexpected Virtue of Ignorance)

movies.overview: All unemployed, Ki-taek's family takes peculiar interest in the wealthy and glamorous Parks for their livelihood until they get entangled in an unexpected incident.
movies.title: Parasite

movies.overview: King T'Challa returns home to the reclusive, technologically advanced African nation of Wakanda to serve as his country's new leader. However, T'Challa soon finds that he is challenged for the throne by factions within his own country as well as without. Using powers reserved to Wakandan kings, T'Challa assumes the Black Panther mantle to join with ex-girlfriend Nakia, the queen-mother, his princess-kid sister, members of the Dora Milaje (the Wakandan 'special forces') and an American secret agent, to prevent Wakanda from being dragged into a world war.
movies.title: Black Panther

movies.overview: An other-worldly story, set against the backdrop of Cold War era America circa 1962, where a mute janitor working at a lab falls in love with an amphibious man being held captive there and devises a plan to help him escape.
movies.title: The Shape of Water

movies.overview: Four sisters come of age in America in the aftermath of the Civil War.
movies.title: Little Women

movies.overview: In the pre-Civil War United States, Solomon Northup, a free black man from upstate New York, is abducted and sold into slavery. Facing cruelty as well as unexpected kindnesses Solomon struggles not only to stay alive, but to retain his dignity. In the twelfth year of his unforgettable odyssey, Solomon’s chance meeting with a Canadian abolitionist will forever alter his life.
movies.title: 12 Years a Slave

movies.overview: "Selma," as in Alabama, the place where segregation in the South was at its worst, leading to a march that ended in violence, forcing a famous statement by President Lyndon B. Johnson that ultimately led to the signing of the Voting Rights Act.
movies.title: Selma

movies.overview: In the 1820s, a frontiersman, Hugh Glass, sets out on a path of vengeance against those who left him for dead after a bear mauling.
movies.title: The Revenant

movies.overview: Aibileen Clark is a middle-aged African-American maid who has spent her life raising white children and has recently lost her only son; Minny Jackson is an African-American maid who has often offended her employers despite her family's struggles with money and her desperate need for jobs; and Eugenia "Skeeter" Phelan is a young white woman who has recently moved back home after graduating college to find out her childhood maid has mysteriously disappeared. These three stories intertwine to explain how life in Jackson, Mississippi revolves around "the help"; yet they are always kept at a certain distance because of racial lines.
movies.title: The Help

movies.overview: The untold story of Katherine G. Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson – brilliant African-American women working at NASA and serving as the brains behind one of the greatest operations in history – the launch of astronaut John Glenn into orbit. The visionary trio crossed all gender and race lines to inspire generations to dream big.
movies.title: Hidden Figures

movies.overview: Dr. Ryan Stone, a brilliant medical engineer on her first Shuttle mission, with veteran astronaut Matt Kowalsky in command of his last flight before retiring. But on a seemingly routine spacewalk, disaster strikes. The Shuttle is destroyed, leaving Stone and Kowalsky completely alone-tethered to nothing but each other and spiraling out into the blackness of space. The deafening silence tells them they have lost any link to Earth and any chance for rescue. As fear turns to panic, every gulp of air eats away at what little oxygen is left. But the only way home may be to go further out into the terrifying expanse of space.
movies.title: Gravity

movies.overview: Chris and his girlfriend Rose go upstate to visit her parents for the weekend. At first, Chris reads the family's overly accommodating behavior as nervous attempts to deal with their daughter's interracial relationship, but as the weekend progresses, a series of increasingly disturbing discoveries lead him to a truth that he never could have imagined.
movies.title: Get Out

movies.overview: A ragtag band of humans band together in the year 2025 to fight legions of monstrous creatures rising from the sea. Using massive piloted robots to combat the alien threat, earth's survivors take the fight to the invading alien force lurking in the depths of the Pacific Ocean. Nearly defenseless in the face of the relentless enemy, the forces of mankind have no choice but to turn to two unlikely heroes -- a washed up former pilot and an untested trainee -- who now stand as earth's final hope against the mounting apocalypse.
movies.title: Pacific Rim

movies.overview: Colorado Springs, late 1970s. Ron Stallworth, an African American police officer, and Flip Zimmerman, his Jewish colleague, run an undercover operation to infiltrate the Ku Klux Klan.
movies.title: BlacKkKlansman

movies.overview: A drama based on the experiences of Agu, a child fighting in the civil war of an unnamed, fictional West African country. Follows the journey of Agu as he's forced to join a group of soldiers. While Agu fears his commander and many of the men around him, his fledgling childhood has been brutally shattered by the war raging through his country, and he is at first torn between conflicting revulsion and fascination. Depicts the mechanics of war and does not shy away from explicit, visceral detail, painting a complex, difficult picture of Agu as a child soldier.
movies.title: Beasts of No Nation

movies.overview: Two academic teenage superstars realize, on the eve of their high school graduation, that they should have worked less and played more. Determined to never fall short of their peers, the girls set out on a mission to cram four years of fun into one night.
movies.title: Booksmart
